title: Before you begin
line: The whole story in six sessions: a map for everything after.
why: Walk the whole cathedral once, quickly, before you go hall by hall.

title: The Old Testament
label: The Old Testament
line: Israel's story: the promise everything else rests on.
why: Every other hall assumes you know this story. It is the way in, at the west door, and it leads straight to the next hall.

later.title: Psalms and wisdom
later.question: How do we pray, think and live in God's world?
texts: Tolstoy, A Confession (Maude, 1921), the chapters of despair where he quotes Ecclesiastes
later.objection: Ecclesiastes and Tolstoy's Confession: is life meaningless? With Psalm 88: does God answer?
later.note: Ends with John 1 and Colossians 1 (Christ as God's Word and Wisdom): the bridge to Who was Jesus?, which follows it.

later.title: How to read the Bible
later.question: How do you read a text so that it reads you?
texts: Guigo II, The Ladder of Monks

rewrite.question: What is the story the Bible tells?
rewrite.note: Raise to the new format (background, commentary, lecture, debate, checks, case so far). Make it the map of the hall: each act points to the journey that goes deeper. Add a two-minute screen on why there are two Testaments ('testament' = covenant; Jeremiah 31; Luke 22:20).

Small addition: Jordan Peterson's psychological reading of Genesis (the 2017 Biblical Series lectures; Maps of Meaning, 1999) as a fourth position in session 1's debate on what kind of writing Genesis is, cited to where he said it.

title: Jesus and the New Testament
label: Jesus and
the New
Testament
line: The life at the centre of it all, and the first Christians.
why: The promise of the Old Testament meets a man from Nazareth. Everything after this turns on who he was.

later.title: The Sermon on the Mount
later.question: What did Jesus teach about how to live?
texts: Augustine, Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount
Tolstoy, The Kingdom of God Is Within You (Garnett)

later.title: The last week and the cross
later.question: What happened in Jerusalem, and did he rise?
later.objection: Did he rise? The alternative explanations at full strength.
later.note: Takes over the cross and resurrection from Who was Jesus?. Tacitus Annals 15.44 is already read in Can I trust the Bible?: point back to it rather than re-reading it. Also absorbs the planned 'Did Jesus rise?' (N. T. Wright and his critics, in our own words).

later.title: Why the cross?
later.question: How can one death save?

later.title: The first Christians
later.question: How did a few followers of a crucified man change an empire?
later.note: Galatians 3 and Romans 4 are already read in Abraham and the promise.

later.title: One root, two branches
later.question: How did Christianity grow out of Judaism, and why did they part?
later.objection: Did the New Testament teach contempt for Jews? Christian anti-Judaism faced squarely.
sessions: A Jewish sect: the first church in Jerusalem
The Temple falls (AD 70), Yavneh and the parting
The case against: did the New Testament teach contempt?
Why keep the Old Testament? Marcion, Irenaeus and the new covenant
The verdict: one olive tree; Jews and Christians today

later.title: What happens at church
later.question: Why do Christians baptise and break bread?

later.title: The end of the story
later.question: Where is history going?
texts: Albert Schweitzer, The Quest of the Historical Jesus (Montgomery, 1910)
later.objection: Failed prophecy: did Jesus expect the end within a generation (Mark 13:30)?
later.note: Closes the hall with its 'make the case' essay: is this story true, and is it mine?

rewrite.question: Who did he claim to be, and was he right?
rewrite.note: Rewrite around his identity: the birth narratives, his claims (Son of Man, Messiah, Mark 2 and 14:62), miracles, prophecy and fulfilment (Isaiah 53 is read in Kings and prophets). Move the cross and the resurrection (Mark 15, 1 Corinthians 15, John 20) to The last week; point back to Can I trust the Bible? for Josephus and Tacitus instead of re-reading them; move Pliny to The first Christians. Objection: 'just a good teacher' / he did not fulfil prophecy. Open with a short screen on the world Jesus was born into: Greek language and ideas, Roman rule. Its case against ('just a good teacher') sets out C. S. Lewis's 'liar, lunatic or Lord' (Mere Christianity, Book 2) in our own words, with its critics.

title: Athens
label: Athens
line: The Greeks: reason, the soul and the good life.
why: The second root of the West. Jerusalem gave it a story; Athens gave it questions and the tools to answer them.

later.title: Homer and the heroes
later.question: What did the Greeks think a great life was?

later.title: Tragedy
later.question: Can suffering teach us?
texts: Sophocles, Oedipus the King and Antigone (Jebb)

later.title: Democracy and its dangers
later.question: Who should rule, and how?

later.title: The first historians
later.question: How did history begin, and what does power do?
texts: Thucydides, the plague and the Melian dialogue (Crawley)

later.title: Number and nature
later.question: How did the Greeks begin to explain the world?

later.title: Socrates
later.question: What is the examined life?

later.title: Plato
later.question: What is real, and what is the soul?

later.title: Aristotle
later.question: What is a thing for, and what is a person for?
later.note: Faces Aristotle's defence of 'natural slaves' honestly.

later.title: Epicureans and Stoics
later.question: How do you find peace?

title: Rome and the First Church
label: Rome and the
First Church
line: Where Athens met Jerusalem, and an empire was changed.
why: Where the three roots meet: Rome's law and order, Athens' reason, and the faith from Jerusalem that changed what the empire valued.

later.title: Rome: Cicero, Virgil and the law
later.question: What did Rome give us?
texts: Cicero, On Duties and the Dream of Scipio

later.title: When Athens met Jerusalem
later.question: Can philosophy and faith meet?

later.title: The martyrs and the empire
later.question: Why did Rome persecute Christians, and how did it end?

later.title: Augustine
later.question: Why are we restless, and what are the two cities?

later.title: The fall of Rome and what survived
later.question: What survives when a civilisation falls?

later.title: Honour, duty and service
later.question: What does a noble life look like today?
texts: Newman, The Idea of a University (the gentleman)

later.title: The art of persuasion
later.question: How do you defend what is true and good?
texts: Lincoln, the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural

title: The Middle Ages
label: The Middle
Ages
why: Monasteries, universities, cathedrals, law and chivalry: the medieval West, its glories and its failures.

later.title: Monks who saved the West
later.question: How did learning survive?

later.title: Reason and revelation
later.question: Can faith and reason agree?

later.title: Cathedrals and universities
later.question: How did the Middle Ages build its schools?
texts: Abelard, The Story of My Misfortunes

later.title: Chivalry: the making of a knight
later.question: What is strength for?
texts: Ramon Llull, The Book of the Order of Chivalry (Caxton)

later.title: The Crusades: what really happened?
later.question: Holy war, or a betrayal of Christ?
texts: Fulcher of Chartres on Urban II at Clermont
later.note: Faced honestly: the hall's case against.

later.title: The rule of law
later.question: Why should even kings be under the law?

later.title: Holy places and holy time
later.question: Why do people set places and times apart?

later.title: Dante
later.question: Where does the road through hell lead?

later.title: The mystics
later.question: Can God be known, not only known about?

title: Reformation and Renaissance
label: Reformation
and
Renaissance
line: 1500–1700: a broken church, a new world, a new science.
why: The age that tore Christendom apart and, out of the wreckage, found religious freedom, human rights and modern science.

later.title: The Reformation
later.question: What was it about, and what did it cost?
texts: Luther, The Freedom of a Christian

later.title: The King James Bible
later.question: How did one translation shape English?
texts: the King James Bible (1611) and 'The Translators to the Reader'

later.title: The New World and the rights of man
later.question: Are all peoples equal before God?
texts: Francisco de Vitoria, On the Indians
later.note: Where universal rights and international law began, as a Christian protest against conquest.

later.title: From wars of religion to toleration
later.question: How did Christians learn to live with difference?

later.title: Shakespeare
later.question: What do the plays know about mercy and grace?

later.title: The poets
later.question: What can poetry say about God?

later.title: Faith and the new science
later.question: Did science and faith go to war?
texts: Galileo, Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina

later.title: Pascal and doubt
later.question: Is it reasonable to bet on God?

title: The Modern World
label: The Modern
World
line: 1700 to today: freedom, its triumphs and its catastrophes.
why: Rights, science, the end of slavery, the death of God and the century of the camps, and what the West must remember to survive.

later.title: Rights and revolutions
later.question: Where do our rights come from?

later.title: The end of slavery
later.question: Why did abolition begin in the Christian West?

later.title: Scotland's Enlightenment
later.question: What did Edinburgh teach the modern world?
texts: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments and The Wealth of Nations

later.title: Hume and the miracles
later.question: Can a reasonable person believe in miracles?
texts: George Campbell, A Dissertation on Miracles (1762)

later.title: Darwin and design
later.question: Does evolution leave room for God?

later.title: The death of God?
later.question: What happens to a world that stops believing?
texts: Tolstoy, A Confession (Maude, 1921), the later chapters: his return through the faith of ordinary people
later.note: The despairing chapters of A Confession are read in Psalms and wisdom (Hall I); here, the road back.

later.title: Dostoevsky
later.question: If there is no God, is everything permitted?

later.title: The twentieth century: what went wrong?
later.question: What happens when the West abandons its foundations?

later.title: After the death of God
later.question: How did Christians answer the twentieth century?

later.title: Is God coming back?
later.question: Why are thinking people turning back to Christianity, and is it enough?
voices: Jordan Peterson (Biblical Series 2017; 12 Rules for Life 2018; We Who Wrestle with God 2024)
Christopher Kaczor and Matthew Petrusek, Jordan Peterson, God, and Christianity (2021)
Justin Brierley, The Surprising Rebirth of Belief in God (2023)
later.objection: Is finding the Bible meaningful the same as believing it true? Kaczor and Petrusek's challenge, and Peterson's 'I act as if God exists'.
later.note: Each session pairs a modern voice (our own words, cited) with the Bible passage or public-domain text they discuss. The Voices profiles of Peterson, Holland, Hirsi Ali, Kingsnorth, McGilchrist and Brierley already exist.

later.title: The world church
later.question: What does Christianity look like beyond Europe?

later.title: In defence of the West
later.question: What is the West, and is it worth defending?
texts: Solzhenitsyn's Harvard address (1978), in our own words
later.note: The capstone: what the West is, its crimes judged by its own principles, the strongest critiques and the answers.

title: The Great Questions
label: The Great
Questions
line: Everything you have learned, brought to the questions that matter most.
why: After the whole story, from Genesis to the modern world, these are your questions: God, being human, suffering, evil, death. Now you have what you need to answer them.

later.title: Who God is: the Creed
later.question: What does the Creed say, and why?
voices: C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity (1952), Book 4, 'Beyond Personality'

later.title: The line through the heart
later.question: Where does evil come from?

later.title: Job
later.question: What does God owe the innocent?

later.title: One way among many?
later.question: How should Christians see other faiths?
texts: Nicholas of Cusa, On the Peace of Faith

rewrite.note: Add the moral argument: C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity Book 1 ('Right and Wrong as a Clue to the Meaning of the Universe'), in our own words, as a lecture section and debate position, with its strongest critics.

Raise to the playbook. Add a session 'Two books by one man': C. S. Lewis, The Problem of Pain (1940) and A Grief Observed (1961), the argument and the grief, in our own words. Add Viktor Frankl (Man's Search for Meaning) and Simone Weil (on affliction) as voices, in our own words. Job stays as its own journey.

title: The Good Life
label: The Good
Life
line: Everything learned, lived: right and wrong, love, work, prayer.
why: Knowing is not enough. This last hall, at the altar, is about becoming the kind of person the whole story was meant to form, and ends with an honest invitation.

later.title: Right and wrong
later.question: Where do right and wrong come from, and how do we know?
texts: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II q.94 (natural law)
Darwin, The Descent of Man, ch. 4 (the moral sense)
voices: C. S. Lewis, The Abolition of Man
later.objection: Morality without God: is conscience only evolved feeling and custom?
later.note: The ethics journey: the four main theories (divine command and natural law, virtue, duty, consequences) side by side, then Nietzsche's attack. Opens the hall, before The four virtues.

later.title: The four virtues
later.question: What are courage, justice, self-control and wisdom?
voices: C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity (1952), Book 3, 'Christian Behaviour'

later.title: Faith, hope and love
later.question: What are the virtues that look beyond us?
voices: C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity (1952), Book 3

later.title: The seven deadly sins
later.question: What quietly shapes us?

later.title: Love, friendship and marriage
later.question: What are the kinds of love, and what is marriage for?
voices: C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves
later.note: Sets out the traditions on sexuality fairly; needs a pastor's review.

later.title: Work and money
later.question: Is work holy, and how much is enough?

later.title: Guilt and forgiveness
later.question: Can we be forgiven, and can we forgive?

later.title: Hard cases
later.question: How do Christians reason about life, death, war and the body?
texts: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II–II q.40 (just war) and q.64
later.objection: Should faith shape the law of a plural society? Mill's harm principle at full strength.
later.note: Abortion, euthanasia, just war and the death penalty, with the traditions' positions set out fairly, including where Christians disagree. Needs a pastor's review.

later.title: Silence
later.question: Why did the saints go into the desert?

later.title: Finding God's will
later.question: How do I know what to do with my life?
texts: Ignatius of Loyola, rules for discernment

later.title: Come and see
later.question: So, is it true, and how would I begin?
voices: C. S. Lewis, Surprised by Joy
later.objection: Why not stay agnostic? The case for suspending judgement, at full strength.
later.note: The last journey in Rose Window: a verdict across all the halls and an honest invitation, never pressure. Its practice is a first step: a visit to church (the Sunday tab) and a week of the daily rhythm.
